content.text:
For a **typical cold**, medicine won’t cure it faster, but it can reduce symptoms. Most colds improve on their own in about **7–10 days**. Antibiotics don’t help because colds are usually viral. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Choose medicine based on your symptoms:**

- **Fever, sore throat, headache, body aches:**  
  Take **acetaminophen** — Tylenol — or **ibuprofen** — Advil/Motrin — as directed on the label. Avoid doubling up: many “multi-symptom” cold medicines already contain acetaminophen. Taking too much can be dangerous. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/safe-use-over-counter-pain-relievers-and-fever-reducers/acetaminophen?utm_source=openai))

- **Stuffy nose:**  
  Try a **saline nasal spray** first. A nasal decongestant spray can help short-term, but don’t use it for more than **3 days** unless a clinician tells you to. If considering oral decongestants, ask a pharmacist/doctor first if you have **high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, prostate problems, are pregnant, or take stimulant/MAOI medications**.

- **Cough:**  
  **Honey** can help calm a cough for adults and children **over 1 year old**. Do **not** give honey to infants under 1 year. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/media/pdfs/2024/04/CommonCold_fact_sheet_508.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
  OTC cough medicines may help some adults, but use only as directed and avoid combining products with the same ingredients.

- **Runny nose/sneezing:**  
  Some people get relief from an **antihistamine**, but it can cause drowsiness and dry mouth.

**Avoid:**  
- **Antibiotics** unless a clinician diagnoses a bacterial infection.  
- Giving OTC cough/cold medicines to young children without medical advice; FDA cautions against acetaminophen or cough/cold medicines in children under **2** without a healthcare provider’s advice, and CDC says OTC cough/cold medicines are not recommended for children under **4**. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/safe-use-over-counter-pain-relievers-and-fever-reducers/health-bulletin-use-caution-pain-relievers-acetaminophen?utm_source=openai))

**Also do:** rest, fluids, humidified air/steam, salt-water gargles, and consider testing for **COVID or flu** if symptoms fit or you’ve been exposed—flu/COVID may have treatments if started early. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Get medical care urgently** if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, dehydration, symptoms that are severe/worsening, fever lasting more than a few days, or if you’re high-risk — pregnant, older adult, immunocompromised, or have serious heart/lung disease.
